idiom_name: claim-set builder + library signer + published verification keys (JWKS / SAML metadata)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep three responsibilities apart. (1) A claim assembler takes subject, attributes and intended audience and produces a canonical profile in which issuer, issued-at, expiry and a replay identifier are filled in by policy rather than by the caller; jti or a SAML assertion ID is single-use only when the consumer records it. (2) A signer transforms that profile into the exact protected representation using a vetted JOSE or XML-DSig implementation, addressing the key by id so algorithms and key material stay inside a keystore, HSM or KMS. (3) A publisher exposes the matching public keys where consumers fetch them and select by key id. For JWTs, golang-jwt/jwt, Nimbus JOSE+JWT, PyJWT and jose implement the JWS layer; for SAML, OpenSAML and equivalent libraries handle XML objects and canonicalisation. In either profile, signature verification is not claim validation: the consumer must still enforce issuer, audience, time conditions, replay rules and protocol-specific binding checks. Inject a clock abstraction for deterministic expiry tests and keep the policy wrapper responsible for the mandatory profile fields.
code_sketch:
issued_at = clock.now()
claims = {iss: issuer, sub: subject, aud: audience,
          iat: issued_at, exp: issued_at + ttl, jti: random_id()}
header = {alg: profile.alg, kid: signer.key_id(), typ: profile.typ}
assertion = sign(profile.serialize(header, claims))  # key stays in KMS/HSM
publish_verification_key(signer.public_key(), signer.key_id())
# consumer: verify signature, then check issuer, audience, time and replay id
pitfalls: Wrong move: let missing expiry or audience default to an empty value; it mints a bearer assertion that is valid everywhere and potentially forever; instead reject issuance until the profile supplies both.

Wrong move: sign with a key before its verification material is published; consumers cannot select a key and every assertion fails closed during rollout; instead publish the new key first and overlap it through rotation.

Wrong move: emit sub on one path and subject on another; consumers silently bind different principals from equivalent assertions; instead version one claim profile and test it as a cross-service contract.

Wrong move: stop after cryptographic verification; a valid signature can still carry the wrong issuer, audience, expiry or replay id; instead perform protocol and claim validation before mapping a principal.

Wrong move: accept alg, jku, x5u or jwk from the token as verification policy; an attacker can select a weaker algorithm or their own key; instead pin algorithms and issuer-anchored key locations server-side.

Wrong move: omit replay storage for SAML assertion IDs or reusable JWT jti values; a captured assertion can be presented repeatedly within its validity window; instead record identifiers for the required acceptance window.

Wrong move: accept an HMAC secret or RSA public key through an untyped key parameter; key-type confusion can turn a public verification key into a signing secret; instead use typed key objects and an algorithm-key allowlist.

Wrong move: accept a SAML signature while reading claims from a different unsigned Assertion node; XML signature wrapping can make attacker-controlled claims win; instead bind the verified reference to the exact assertion consumed and validate its conditions.

Wrong move: canonicalise or mutate XML after signing; equivalent-looking whitespace or namespace changes alter XML-DSig input and make interoperability fail; instead preserve the signed tree and use the profile's explicit canonicalisation method.

Wrong move: translate an upstream assertion by copying its entire claim set; PII and audience-specific claims spread to every downstream service; instead define a target profile and copy only claims the target audience needs.
sources: Steel, Nagappan & Lai, Core Security Patterns: Best Practices and Strategies for J2EE, Web Services, and Identity Management (2005) - ch. 12 'Securing the Identity', Identity Management Security Patterns: Assertion Builder Pattern (with SSO Delegator and Credential Tokenizer); SAML assertion types and XML signatures in ch. 7.
